pr_title: repart: Don't descend into directories assigned to other partitions
pr_body:
Let's say we have the following repart definitions files root.conf
and home.conf:

```
[Partition]
Type=root
CopyFiles=/
```

```
[Partition]
Type=home
CopyFiles=/home
```

Currently, we'd end up copying /home to both the root partition and
the home partition. To prevent this from happening, let's adopt a
new policy when copying files for a partition: We won't copy any
files/directories that appear in the CopyFiles= list of another
partition, unless that directory explicitly appears in our own
CopyFiles= list.

This way, we prevent copying /home twice into the root and home
partition, but should a user really want that behavior, they can
have it by adding /home to the CopyFIles= list of the root partition
as well.

Fixes #24786
pr_comments: So, as mentioned, I still think it would be much nicer if we would alway implicitly exclude the top-level referenced inode from the denylist in copy_tree(), i.e. only check the denylist for enumerated dentrys, not for referenced inodes. You could have a single global denylist then, and this patch would be a lot prettier and more minimal!

> So, as mentioned, I still think it would be much nicer if we would alway implicitly exclude the top-level referenced inode from the denylist in copy_tree(), i.e. only check the denylist for enumerated dentrys, not for referenced inodes. You could have a single global denylist then, and this patch would be a lot prettier and more minimal!

It took a while before I got it, but you're right, this is a lot simpler, reworked the PR, PTAL!

While the denylist implementation is in good order now, what we put into the denylist is way too broad. I'd like to enable this by default, so we should only do this for a minimal amount of things by default. Specifically, I'm thinking we only employ a denylist when we encounter a root partition, and we add all the mount points of nested partitions to the denylist.
We only skip mount points of nested partitions now, and don't prevent users from copying files around multiple times outside of that.
Can you add some tests to the repart integration test? Also needs a rebase

issue_context.title: repart should support a global version of CopyFiles=
issue_context.body:
### Component

_No response_

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

Let's say I have a directory tree that I want to move to a disk image with a root partition and a home partition. If I try to use the following config files, I will run into issues:

```
[Partition]
Type=root
CopyFiles=/
````

```
[Partition]
Type=home
CopyFiles=/home
```

Since the files from /home will end up in both the root partition and the home partition.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Instead of copying files per partition, I want to copy them all at once. What I figure we should do is format all the partitions with filesystems, mount them all at their canonical mount point, and then copy all files at once from a directory tree. This makes sure that all files end up in the right partition.

I'd probably go about this by adding a --copy-files switch that takes a directory. If --copy-files is configured, after formatting the filesystems, repart would mount them all and copy the files from the --copy-files directory (target == "/").

Now, you could end up in a scenario where no root partition is configured, so I figure we should do all the mounts in a temporary directory, and create upper level directories as needed if there is no partition for them. That way, if only a usr partition is configured, all the files outside of the usr partition would simply end up being thrown away when the temporary directory is deleted. The only annoying thing is that this isn't super efficient, since we might be copying files unnecessarily, but it's not impossible to optimize later (e.g. only copy files that are prefixed with one of the partition mount point directories or such).

### Describe alternatives you've considered

We could add an ExcludeFiles= switch to repart to not copy anything under the configured excludes, but that requires a lot of manual configuration from the user to figure out the required excludes based on the other partitions that are configured, which would lead to a lot of manual hassle. The proposed solution requires zero extra configuration from the user, just configure a set of partitions, and repart will automatically make sure that every directory from the directory tree ends up in the right partition.

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

main
comments: Isn't that something to just do with `systemd-dissect --copy-to`? I mean that does exactly what you are asking for here, no?
Yes, but that means I can't use the verity support I just added to repart anymore

I see.

What about just adding ExcludeCopy= or so? so that in the root fs you say CopyFiles=/ and then ExcludeCopy=/home?

Yes but configuring all of this manually from mkosi is not great, I think we should do this by default in repart. If a home partition is configured, it probably does not make sense to copy files from /home into the root partition. (And the same for all the other partition types)

so, wouldn't it make sense to call repart twice? i.e. first to create the basic structure. then you'd do `systemd-tmpfiles --image=` and `systemd-dissect --copy-to` and then you would call `systemd-repart` again, to add in verity?

Hmm, that would actually work I think, and just not use CopyFiles= at all.

But with that approach, I'd like to be able to tell repart what partitions to create in each run, since I want the user to be able to supply all partition definitions in the same directory, but that could include verity, so we'd need a CLI switch to tell repart whether to apply the verity stuff or not.

i mean, sooner or later people might want to run the whole series:

1. systemd-repart --image= (for basic partitions)
2. systemd-tmpfiles --image= (for basic hierarchy)
3. systemd-dissect --copy-to (to populate hierarchy)
4. systemd-sysusers --image= to create users
5. systemd-firstboot --image= (to provision basic settings)
6. bootctl --image= (to install boot loader)
7. systemd-repart (to finalize verity)

It probably would make sense to teach systemd-firstboot and systemd-dissect some additional tricks to make this comprehensive.

i.e. systemd-dissect should probably gain a tool "--reset-timestamp" or so, for resetting all times back to zero, and systemd-firstboot should probably gain "--generalize" or something like that which removes machine-id/random seeds and stuff.

> But with that approach, I'd like to be able to tell repart what partitions to create in each run, since I want the user to be able to supply all partition definitions in the same directory, but that could include verity, so we'd need a CLI switch to tell repart whether to apply the verity stuff or not.

Sounds reasonable. Maybe add --filter-partitions= or so, where you can list part type uuids, either as allowlist or as denylist or so, and we'd not operate on what is listed.

I was thinking of just adding a --verity switch really. This seems pretty specific to the verity use case, not sure if we should make it more generic than that.

Also, I figure we should still create the verity partitions, just not format them yet and don't set the UUID yet. That way, the partitions are still applied as if repart was only executed once, the only thing that's left to do in the second run is to format the verity stuff in the verity partitions.

Also for completeness, while this approach will work for almost all our usecases, it won't work for squashfs or other read-only filesystems, since that has to be done with CopyFiles=.

I wonder if we should stick with the current approach (at least for final images) in mkosi after all, if gpt is requested, run repart once beforehand, mount everything with systemd-dissect, run all the other installation steps, unmount, and run repart again to format any verity partitions if needed.

read-only filesystems are still really weird though. Ideally they'd support some kind of staging area, so that you can write to them as like any other filesystem, and then have a finalize command after which it becomes compressed and read-only. Without that, maybe we need some kind of hybrid approach. e.g. tell repart not to format squashfs partitions immediately, just like the verity ones, and simply write to directories on the host filesystem during the host install phase, and then copy to the squashfs when running repart a second time. The issue with that is that you run into the CopyFiles= limitation I'm reporting here again. So you'd still need some kind of automatic exclude so that files don't end up duplicated across squashfs partitions. 

There's also minimized images. Those probably need explicit support from repart as well. The way it happens in mkosi is we generate a filesystem, minimize it, and then use the minimized size to accurately size the partition. I suppose for mkosi that would mean doing the same as with read-only filesystems, write to directories on the host system, and then when repart is executed a second time, format and populate the partition's filesystem outside of the disk image, minimize it, and use that size to accurately size the partition, and then use the minimized filesystem as a CopyBlocks= source to populate the partition. But again here, when populating the minimized filesystem, we'll run into the same CopyFiles= issue I mentioned here again. So we'll probably need some special handling for root partitions in repart to exclude files that already have a dedicated partition.

The question is whether it should be configured by the user via e.g. CopyExclude= or whether repart should try to figure it out itself.

Another idea would be to have two separate "stages" in repart, "staging" and "finalize". "finalize" would be enabled with --finalize, and "staging" would be enabled with --staging.

In "staging" mode, we would not format verity, replace any read-only filesystems with ext4 instead, and calculate sizes for partitions without taking into account whether they're supposed to be minimized. This staging image can then be mounted with systemd-dissect and populated as usual. Then, when we call repart a second time in "finalize" mode, any partitions that are configured to be minimized are minimized, other partitions are moved around to accommodate the new minimized partitions, the ext4 filesystems are mounted and used as root for the actual read-only filesystem mkfs binaries and verity partitions are formatted.

This approach would mean that regardless of whether read-only or minimized partitions are used, the logic to populate the partitions with systemd-dissect and systemd-tmpfiles is the same and we don't need to use CopyFiles= for read-only or minimized partitions to make things work. Using ext4 as a staging area for the read-only filesystems shouldn't be a problem as these can't be populated in place anyway so the original source tree is always going to come from another filesystem regardless, whether's it's an ext4 filesystem generated by repart or the host filesystem.

This also plays well with caching in mkosi, if we're building cache images, we'd simply skip running repart the second time with --finalize and just cache the staging image and reuse that when available.

So the replace squashfs with ext4 idea isn't exactly trivial, since you can't just convert the ext4 to squashfs in place, you'd have to generate the squashfs outside of the disk image and then copy it back in over the ext4 staging filesystem, which seems rather inefficient and ugly, but it's the best I can come up with that still allows us to keep a unified interface to populate a disk image regardless of what options are used for the partitions.

So staging mode would mean:
- Ignore to be implemented `Minimize=` setting on partitions
- Replace read-only filesystems with ext4 to be used as a staging area
- Don't generate verity hash/sig partitions

And finalize mode would mean:
- Minimize existing partitions with `Minimize=` setting enabled. For ext2, ext3 and ext4, `resize2fs` should work in place, for btrfs, we'll have to use a temporary loop device to recreate the btrfs filesystem and pass the --shrink option to mkfs.btrfs. Other filesystems we'd just not support minimization.
- Compact partitions after minimization (reduce size of minimized partitions, and move offsets of following partitions forward to take up the space freed by minimization, but make sure padding is still respected)
- For partitions with read-only filesystems configured, mount the existing partition, create a new loop device with same size as the existing partition, format that new loop device with the read-only filesystem using the existing mounted partition root as the source tree, and afterwards replace the existing partition with the contents of the loop device.
- Generate verity hash/sig partitions

I'd probably make the finalize mode a completely separate codepath just after we've loaded the partition table so that in finalize mode we only do the mentioned things and absolutely nothing else.

This approach wouldn't be the most efficient one, but it seems like it would be easy to use:

- run repart once with mode = "staging", 
- populate the staging image using all the other tools with the --image switch
- run repart again with mode = "finalize" on the staging image

note that homed already contains offline calls to resize2fs. we could generalize, add similar support for btrfs offline resize and then implement a "Minimize=" option in repart with it. Might be kinda nice, since it could be a "smart" minimize, i.e. a bisection loop that takes SizeMin= and SizeMax= into account.

so, let me sort stuff we really need to cover:

a. create partitions
b. create directories
c. create subvolumes
d. copy in OS files (depends on c)
e. minimize fs (depends on b, c, d)
f. encrypt fs (depends on e)
g. calculate verity fs (depends on e)
h. sign verity (depends on g)
i. write verity root hash to partition uuids (depends on e)
j. run tmpfiles on it (depends on d)
k. run sysusers on it (depends on d)
l. run bootctl on it (depends on a)
m. run firstboot on it (depends on d)
n. generate UKI with root hash (depends on e)
o. copy UKI in (depends on a)

which is quiet a complex dependency tree...

and it's not even complete, since I guess populating and sealing of root fs via verity must be done before we write UKI into ESP.

I am currently leaning towards this:

1. try to prepare as much as we can in a staging tree, and let repart package it up.
2. since we cannot create btrfs subvolumes in a staging tree most likely (given it can be backed by a non-btrfs fs), this probably then means we should add MakeSubvolume= to repart files after all, to complement MakeDirectory=. And maybe do that in a syntax of `<name>:<flags>`. i.e. `MakeSubvolume=/foobar:ro`. This would need to implemented carefully in repart: i.e. create the subvolume before copying in files, mark it read only afterwards.
3. add a MinimizeFileSystem= natively to repart, for creating minimal file systems. Question is how to implement that best. One idea is via bisection of making/populating the fs. Other idea is via bisection of offline shrinking. 

With that we could first arrange everything in a staging dir, even run tmpfiles/sysusers/firsboot on it. The we'd glue it all together with repart, minimized. And then finally install kernel/boot laoder into a fixed size ESP.

so here's another idea I just had, which I think I kinda like.

what about introducing a set of xattrs that copy_tree() optionall honours, that tweak its behaviour. something like this:

```
metacopy.subvol=1
metacopy.rosubvol=1
metacopy.chattr=0x4711
metacopy.stop=1
```

Under the assumption that all relevant file systems support xattrs these days but they differ on support of subvol/rosubvol/chattr these xattrs could carry additional info that we'd honour when copying such a tree onto a file system that supports these special concepts.

Specifically, when encountering `metacopy.subvol=1` or `metacopy.rosubvol=1` on a directory inode, CopyFiles= (and similar calls in tmpfiles) will try to create the dir as a subvolume, and use a dir as fallback. When encountering `metacopy.rosubvol=1` it would mark the subvolume as read-only after use. When encountering `metacopy.chattr=…` it would set chattr flags on the copied inode. And then, `metacopy.stop=1` would tell the copy logic to exclude the inode this is set on from copying unless it is the root of what shall be copied.

This would tne allow us prepare everything in the staging tree: create the whole hierarchy in a staging tree, set some special values, and then have repart just glue it all together, with the right concepts.

What do you think?

interpretaion of these concepts would be guarded by new flags in `CopyFlags`. i.e. `COPY_HONOUR_XATTR_METACOPY_SUBVOL`, `COPY_HONOUR_XATTR_METACOPY_CHATTR` and `COPY_HONOUR_XATTR_METACOPY_STOP`. And then we would set all three for CopyFiles= in repart and `C` lines of tmpfiles.d at least.

And there probably should be COPY_HONOUR_XATTR_METACOPY_STRIP or so as another flag: when set we'd drop all xattrs starting with `metacopy` when copying xattrs

That still means mkosi has to figure out where it should set `metacopy.stop` on depending on which partitions are configured in repart. I would very much prefer if mkosi didn't have to concern itself with all that logic. Same with subvolumes really, the user should just be able to supply a tmpfiles snippet with the subvolume stuff in it and the only thing mkosi should have to do is pass that file to systemd-tmpfiles when it executes it. The only thing mkosi I want mkosi to be doing ideally is to just run the tools in the right order with the right configuration and leave everything else to the systemd tooling.

That's why I like the staging idea so much, mkosi just has to run systemd-repart in staging mode, mount the resulting image with systemd-dissect, and it has a ready-to-go root mount that it can start populating (run package manager, tmpfiles, firstboot, ...). All the files will automatically end up in the right partitions without any involvement required from mkosi's side.

The only tradeoff is that we need a "staging" concept in repart, because partitions can't always be minimized in place, minimization can only happen after population, and read-only filesystems need a staging area so they can be populated, so we have to put another filesystem in there temporarily to allow populating the read-only filesystem and then use that as the source for the actual read-only filesystem later.
what i dislike about the idea of staging-on-disk-image as opposed to staging-on-host-fs is the sizing question. It means you have to pick a size first.

so, i started out with the staging-on-disk-image model with mkosi, and as we kept adding stuff such as minimization and squashfs and tarball output and such i figured its kinda broken to try to hard to stick to it, and instead we should really go for the staging-on-host-fs concept everywhere, to make things systematic again, and unify codepaths again.

so if you don't like the `metacopy.stop=1` idea. what about this idea: make the copy logic in repart smarter. automatically stop descending further into recursive copy once we hit one of inodes that we already would copy otherwise.

implementation would be like this: before copying anything, do stat() on all inodes directly pointed to by CopyFiles=, and collect their st_dev/st_ino into a `Set` object. Then, pass that to copy_tree() as a denylist: whenever we descent the tree and reach an inode matching an entry in the `Set` we'll skip it.

that should nicely cover it, no?

Yeah, that's similar to what I was thinking to solve that problem without doing staging (I was going to use paths, but the inode stuff is way more interesting). 

Still, I'd very much like to avoid reinventing tmpfiles with xattrs. What about running tmpfiles as a library before populating the filesystems (except for read-only filesystems) in repart?

EDIT: Nvm that wouldn't work because it needs all partitions to be mounted in the right place

What about adding something to tmpfiles that lets it set the xattrs based on what's in the the tmpfiles snippets? So that we can run it on the staging area to just have it set xattrs. And then the copy logic can pick up on the xattrs.

i would run tmpfiles --root= on the staging area dir anyway. It will apply xattrs, it might apply more. if some of the stuff cannot be picked up by CopyFiles=, then so so be it, but xattrs at the very least are covered.
Yes, but for the stuff it can't apply, wouldn't it be great if it could set the `metacopy` xattrs instead? So that it can be picked up later by repart?
sure, i guess we could teach tmpfiles.d to generate these metacopy xattrs indeed. but probably should be optional

One thing I'm worried about is that incremental mode is going to slow down quite a bit in mkosi when building disk images, since we have to copy the full staging tree to the disk image every time if we do staging outside of the disk image itself.

I first thought about doing shenanigans with btrfs subvolumes and btrfs send/receive, but that's awfully filesystem specific. So I figured, what if we added casync support to sysupdate and used sysupdate when in incremental mode to update an existing disk image?

So we'd populate the new staging area of the final image, optionally based on a cached version of the staging tree. And then if we're building a disk image and one already exists, instead of building it from scratch with repart, we update a casync store based on the staging tree, and then use sysupdate to deploy the update to the disk image, copying only what's necessary instead of the full contents.

review_comments: please add a unit test to cover the deny list

@DaanDeMeyer this one is unaddressed, it would be good to have a unit test case here that covers the case where denylist isn't NULL, as sanity check - doesn't need to be overly complex, just to ensure nothing obvious breaks

I'm not sure if that matters, but now we'll have e.g.
```
{ SD_GPT_ROOT_ARM64,  "root-arm64", ARCHITECTURE_ARM64, .designator = PARTITION_ROOT_OTHER },
{ SD_GPT_ROOT_NATIVE,   "root",            native_architecture(),          .designator = PARTITION_ROOT            },
```
Which means that on arm64, the root partition in the first definition is labeled as `PARTITION_ROOT_OTHER`. This could be confusing… Maybe "OTHER" should be changed to "ARCH" ?

I added descriptions to tell what these actually mean. I don't think changing the name is going to help much. We should probably get rid of the secondary/other enum variants altogether, keep track of all architectures while parsing the partition table, and just at the end figure out the ones we actually want in preference of primary architecture, then secondary, then any other, but let's leave this for another PR

why have PARTITION_LINUX_GENERIC?

linux generic partitions do not have an inherent purpose, they only acquire one if they are is no partition with a proper purpose on a medium, and they are basically the only partition that could be considered a root fs.

Thus, I would argue this should not be a designator of its own, because we will never use it as such. We'll use it as PARTITION_ROOT only.

I think the GptPartitionType .designator field should just be set to _PARTITION_DESIGNATOR_INVALID for partitions of this type, because they really have no inherent designated purpose. And afaics your patch you never actually make use of PARTITION_LINUX_GENERIC except for setting it, hence nothing is lost.

(similar PARTITION_USER_HOME actually)

i would argue you can just drop these two definitions without any change in behaviour

hmm, I am not sure I follow here. So here's what I had in mind:

Taking inspiration from `context_open_copy_block_paths()` add a function `context_open_copy_files_paths()`, that iterates through all partitions, and opens the source inodes to copy from, writing an fd for each top-level inode fd into a new field `p->copy_files_fd`. At the same time fstat() the file, and build up the denylist. When this new function `context_open_copy_files_paths()` is complete we thus have opened/pinned all top-level source inodes, and built a complete denylist based on their inode info. 

Then in a later step, actaully iterate throught the partitions again, now execute the copy routine, each time passing in the already open inode fd, plus the complete deny list.

I thin this would be relatively pretty because it mirrors the copy_blocks logic, and we have a global denylist for all operations.

Does this make sense?

That seems to result in a overly restrictive denylist no?

Let's say I have the following in one partition definition:

```
CopyFiles=/etc/fstab:/home/<user>/fstab-copy
CopyFiles=/etc
```

Just because we copy /etc/fstab to some location in the home directory doesn't mean that we don't want to copy it to /etc/fstab anymore.

I would very much prefer to have a minimal denylist per partition rather than a global one. We generally don't want to prevent users copying files to wherever they want, but only want to intervene when we're 99% sure the behavior doesn't make sense, and to me in this case that's only when we start duplicating full partitions into other partitions, so I'd like to just prevent that from happening but nothing else, at least not without explicit opt-in from the user.

Had another look and I figure we can make the denylist global instead of per partition, that just means that we never copy any nested partitions into another partition, in practice, the behavior should be exactly the same.

I would prefer to stick to just excluding nested partition mount points instead of everything from CopyFiles= by default. If we need more, let's make it opt-in via an option.
